Note 1: 24 longitudinally studied HIV-1 (clades A1 or D)-chronically-infected Kenyan subjects were tested for CTL response to 9-mer overlapping p24 peptides.  Epitope mapping was assessed not just by IFN-γ EliSpot assays, but by multiparametric flow cytometry of intracellular cytokine staining for IL-2, tumor necrosis factor (TNF-α), chemokine macrophage inflammatory protein 1β (MIP-1β) and degranulation marker CD107a, as well as by proliferation assays.  50/69 epitope-specific responses detected were IFN-γ negative.  Several epitope responses had polyfunctional (33%) and proliferative (19%) components.  Long term non progressors (LTNP) had more polyfunctional responses of greater magnitude and proliferation than normal progressors (NP).
Note 2: 16 subjects were tested specifically with 126 putative epitopes, 50 of which were confirmed. Clade A1 epitope iSPRTLNAW, corresponds to B consensus of the same sequence, and elicited a single IL-2 response in one ART-treated subject. Note 1: NL4-3 Gag polyprotein random mutagenesis, high-throughput fitness profiling and in silico prediction of MHC-peptide binding affinity revealed that mutations in CTL epitopes presented by protective MHC-I alleles, vs. non-protective alleles, showed greater loss of experimental replicative capacity and lower levels of predicted reduction in MHC-I binding affinity. Together, these two variables could predict protectiveness of MHC-I alleles in a linear regression model. Analyses of intraperson viral evolution in 4 LTNP vs. 4 paired progressor subjects further supported paper conclusions.
Note 2: After mutagenesis and passaging through human T cells, 49 single nucleotide mutations were observed in epitope SPRTLNAWV (known to bind to B0702) with a log transformation of mean fitness score, relative to NL4-3, of -0.4252.

Note 1: In order to dissect whether natural control of HIV-1 infection is due to infection with a defective virus or whether it is due to host factors, 2 transmission pairs were studied and compared to an elite suppressor transmission pair with defective virus. Note 1: To correlate evolving HIV-1 populations with HLA-A2 restricted immune responses for epitopes in Gag, Pol, Env and Nef, 11 treatment-naive subjects were longitudinally studied.  Results show that increased viral load is often associated with broad CTL responses early in infection that persist as an "immunological footprint".  Conversely, early, restricted responses may help limit viral load.  Phylogenetic and functional evidence of viral escape is seen in Gag, Nef and Pol.  Gag and Nef show flanking epitope changes restricted by non-HLA-A2 alleles. As far as modes of viral adaptation, CTL responses were seen to develop both against static viral populations resulting in viral evolution to HLA-A2 as well as against existing mutants resulting in reselection of consensus B-like variants.  This study reinforces that CTL immune responses detected are not necessarily beneficial to patients, but may be "footprints" from early effective responses that the virus has since escaped.

Dual color EliSpot testing for IL-2 and IFN-γ was used to determine whether CTL restricted by MHC Class I alleles associated with slow progression to disease, viz. B*57 and B*27, had a more poly-functional profile than other CD8+ cells in a treatment-naive cohort from Montreal.  B*57/B*27-restricted CTL producing IL-2 or IFN-γ or IL-2/IFN-γ, were similar in both slow progressors (SP) and progressors.  Other non-protective MHC-I-restricted CTL producing both IL-2/IFN-γ, were greater in number in SP than progressors.
Note 2: Within SP, peptides restricted by both protective and non-protective MHC-I alleles elicited CTL with the same functional profile.  For progressors, peptides and epitopes restricted by protective B*57/B*27 alleles stimulated a higher proportion of dual-(IL-2/IFN-γ)secreting CTL.

Note 1: Variants of Gag, Env, and Nef epitopes were studied in one subject over >10 years of infection. A set of known HLA A*0201- and B*0702-restricted epitopes, plus additional predicted epitopes, was assembled. Epitope and variant responses were studied from 4 timepoints post-seroconversion (SC): early infection post-SC (0-2.8 yrs), late infection post-SC (3.25-7.8 yrs), early ART treatment (8.3-10.1 yrs), and late ART treatment. Despite evolutionary changes, CD8+ T cells could still be primed to HIV-1 variants. The percent of epitope variants inducing HIV-1-specific memory T cell responses peaked early post-SC, then declined and remained minimal shortly after establishment of viral set point. Peptide variants with medium binding affinity were more frequent than variants with low or high binding affinity but variants with different MHC class I binding capabilities induced equally broad memory T cell responses. A trimodal pattern in the breadth of T cell memory was seen, at early SC before viral set point, and then two peaks during later infection prior to commencing cART.
Note 2: TLNAWVKVV was 1 of 7 epitopes with a positive correlation between predicted and observed MHC affinity. TLNAWVKVV had a pattern of transient changes in the dominance of variants, with the founder variant eventually being more dominant.

To identify immunogenically optimized peptide epitopes for use in vaccines, two strategies were used. The first studied rare mutant epitopes that were effective in generating a cross-reactive immune response against a range of mutants.  The second method was to use a synthetic combinatorial library of peptides and screen for highly effective responses against one epitope (TV9, TLNAWVKVV) and its mutants.  Candidate epitopes were tested in HLA-A2 transgenic mice as well as ex vivo human lymphocytes.
Note 2: Natural TV9 mutants tested in transgenic HLA-A*02 mice showed the following responses - the common mutant V9I, TLNAWVKVi was less immunogenic and had low cross-reactivity.  TLNAWVKaV (most cross-reactive) and TLNAWVKai were highly immunogenic and cross-reactive to the consensus.  Other rare mutants were TfNAWVKVV, TLNAWVKVl, TLNArVKVV, TLNAWiKVi, TsNAWVKVi and TLNAWVKcV.
Note 3: Synthetic library mimics chosen were TvNAWnKdV, TLNAWwyaV, TLNAWnKaV, TLNAWnyaV (most immunogenic), TLNAWwydV, TvNAWnyaV, TvNAWwyaV, TvsAvwydV, TLNAWnydV, TLsAWnyaV, TLNAWwKaV, TLsAvwKaV, TLsAWwyaV, TLsAWnydV, TvNAWwKdV and TLNAvwKaV.

Note 4: The impact on replication capacity of H219Q capsid mutation, a compensatory mutation for T242N was minimal. Note 1: Detailed characterization of CD8+ T cells from 12 post-acute-HIV-1-infection untreated subjects identified distinct features of HLA-B*57:01-restricted responses suggesting reduced T cell exhaustion, but these differences diminished with disease progression.
